results.corrected_extracted: Egger tests suggested possible publication bias for short-term working memory (t=2.19, df=10, p=.05) and learning efficiency (t=2.76, df=15, p=.01). After trim-and-fill, short-term working memory shrank to −0.04 (95% CI −0.26 to 0.18; still non-significant; main estimate −0.19), and learning efficiency stayed significant at −0.40 (95% CI −0.52 to −0.28; main estimate −0.47), which the authors describe as unchanged in magnitude.
results.note: What was wrong: −0.40 was presented as a reduction although the authors call learning efficiency unchanged, and the working-memory result was omitted. The Discussion (p. 748) contradicts the Results by saying working memory did not change appreciably under trim-and-fill.

results.corrected_extracted: At follow-up (Table 4), abstainers' global T-score (50.1) no longer differed significantly from controls' (52.8; the authors call them no longer distinguishable, p > 0.05), but abstainers scored significantly below controls on executive functions (50.9 vs 54.3) and working memory (48.4 vs 53.4). At baseline (Table 3) neither domain differed significantly between abstainers and controls (executive 47.0 vs 49.5; working memory 47.2 vs 50.5), so for these two domains the significant gap appeared at follow-up rather than persisting from baseline.

results.corrected_extracted: Subgroup analyses were post hoc. For psychosis, most evidence came from cross-sectional studies, which the authors rate as high quality; significant associations were seen across criminal-justice, drug-treatment and psychiatric settings and in population-level hospital admissions, and these examples include cohort studies (drug-treatment cohort [29], psychiatric inpatient cohort [39], California hospital-admissions cohort [40]).

results.corrected_extracted: For comprehension knowledge only, the group difference depended on risk-of-bias rating (Qbet 7.69, df 1, p=.006): −0.67 SD (95% CI −0.92 to −0.43) in high risk-of-bias studies vs −0.09 SD (95% CI −0.42 to 0.24) in unclear risk-of-bias studies. No other domain differed by rating, and removing the high risk-of-bias studies left the results unchanged. The authors note that retained methamphetamine users may have been healthier than those who dropped out, so attrition may have somewhat attenuated the group differences.
results.note: What was wrong: the −0.67/−0.09 split was presented as general, but it applies only to comprehension knowledge. The passage is under Subgroup Analyses, not the sensitivity analysis (which found no change); the attrition point is in Summary and Conclusions.
